Rāma.gloss: Prince of Ayodhyā. The story of his exile and return is the Rāmāyaṇa.

Sītā.gloss: Rāma's wife, carried away to Laṅkā by Rāvaṇa.

Lakṣmaṇa.gloss: Rāma's younger brother, who followed him into the forest and did not go home.

Hanumān.gloss: Son of Vāyu the wind, and Rāma's messenger. Also, across a different epic, Bhīma's brother.

Laṅkā.gloss: The island kingdom across the water, ruled by Rāvaṇa.

vānaras.gloss: The forest people of the Rāmāyaṇa — usually pictured as monkeys.

Nala.gloss: A name shared by two figures in this collection: the vānara engineer who directs the Setu in the Rāmāyaṇa, and King Nala of Niṣadha in the Mahābhārata's Damayantī story.

Śabarī.gloss: A forest woman who waited most of her life for Rāma to pass her door.

Jaṭāyu.gloss: An old vulture, and a friend of Rāma's father, who tried to stop Rāvaṇa alone.

Guha.gloss: King of the Niṣādas and an intimate friend of Rāma, who receives him at the Gaṅgā during the exile.

Śravaṇa.gloss: A boy who carried his blind parents across the country in two baskets on a pole.

Kṛṣṇa.gloss: Raised among cowherds in Vraja. The boy in these stories is the same person as the sixty-year-old in the Mahābhārata.

Vraja.gloss: The cattle country around Mathurā where Kṛṣṇa grew up.

Govardhana.gloss: The hill that fed the village — grass, water, shade. In one story it is treated as a person, so we count it as one.

Indra.gloss: King of the gods; he sends the rain, and expects to be thanked for it.

Dhruva.gloss: A five-year-old who was told he could not sit on his father's lap, and walked into the forest instead. He is the pole star.

Prahlāda.gloss: A boy who would not stop saying what he believed, in a house where saying it was dangerous.

Gajendra.gloss: An elephant king, caught by the foot in a lake, who was strong for a very long time and then wasn't.

Sudāmā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's poorest friend, who walked a long way to visit him and could not bring himself to ask for anything.

Bhīma.gloss: The strongest of the five Pāṇḍava brothers — and, like Hanumān, a son of Vāyu.

Arjuna.gloss: The archer among the Pāṇḍavas; in Droṇa's bird test he narrows his attention from the bird to its head.

Yudhiṣṭhira.gloss: Eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, and the one the crane at the lake chose to question.

Droṇa.gloss: The teacher of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas. He is not always admirable, and we do not pretend otherwise.

Ekalavya.gloss: A forest boy who taught himself archery from a clay statue of a teacher who had refused him.

Karṇa.gloss: Born with armour fused to his skin, and unable to say no to anyone who asked him for something.

Draupadī.gloss: Wife of the five Pāṇḍavas, and the keeper of the vessel that fed anyone who came.

Abhimanyu.gloss: Arjuna's son, who learned how to get into the spiral formation and never learned how to get out.

Nachiketā.gloss: A boy, maybe nine or ten, who out-waited and out-argued Death.

Yama.gloss: Lord of death — and, on the evidence of this story, a very good host.

Śvetaketu.gloss: A boy who came home from twelve years of study rather pleased with himself, and was handed a lump of salt.

Uddālaka.gloss: Śvetaketu's father, and the best teacher in the Upaniṣads — he never once answers his own question.

Satyakāma.gloss: A boy who told his teacher the one thing he was afraid to say, and was accepted for saying it.

Agni.gloss: Fire. In one story he is asked to burn a single blade of grass, and cannot.

Vāyu.gloss: The wind. Father of Hanumān in one epic and of Bhīma in another — which makes them brothers.

Gaṇeśa.gloss: The elephant-headed son of Śiva and Pārvatī, who won a race around the world without leaving the room.

Pūsalār.gloss: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He built a temple without owning a single stone.

Tiruniṉṟavūr.gloss: A town outside Chennai. Pūsalār's temple is there, in a manner of speaking.

Kāñchipuram.gloss: The Pallava capital. The stone temple in this story is still standing there.

Rājasiṃha.gloss: The Pallava king who built the Kailāsanātha temple at Kāñchipuram around thirteen hundred years ago.

Śiva.gloss: In these stories, usually the one who turns up in person and does something nobody expected.

Nāyaṉmārs.gloss: Sixty-three Tamil Śaiva saints — potters, washermen, kings, hunters, farmers — whose lives Sēkkiḻār set down in the twelfth century.

Āḻvārs.gloss: Twelve Tamil Vaiṣṇava poet-saints. One of them was a woman, one a highwayman, and three of them met in a doorway in the rain.

Periya Purāṇam.gloss: Sēkkiḻār's twelfth-century book of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. There is no Sanskrit version of it.

Sēkkiḻār.gloss: The twelfth-century Chola minister who wrote down the lives of all sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs.

Āṇḍāḷ.gloss: The only woman among the twelve Āḻvārs, and the one who tried the garland on first.

Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār.gloss: One of three women among the Nāyaṉmārs, and the earliest. She asked to be given a shape nobody would find beautiful, and got it.

Srīraṅgam.gloss: The great island temple on the Kāverī, and the one a singer was carried into on a priest's shoulders.

Kailāsa.gloss: Śiva's mountain. In one story someone gets his hands underneath it.

Rāvaṇa.gloss: King of Laṅkā. A scholar, a musician, and — in the Jain retelling — not a demon at all.

Nārada.gloss: A wandering sage who turns up, says one thing, and leaves before the argument starts. He is almost never the villain and almost always the cause.

Kārttikeya.gloss: Śiva's older son — fast, armed with a spear, riding a peacock. In Tamil country he is Murugan, and the hills are his.

Pārvatī.gloss: Śiva's wife, and the mother in these two boys' house. Daughter of the mountain, which is worth remembering when someone races around the world.

Palani.gloss: A hill in Tamil Nadu where Kārttikeya went to sulk, and stayed. People still climb it.

Setu.gloss: The bridge of stones thrown across the sea to Laṅkā. You can still see a line of shoals where it is said to have run.

Jāmbavān.gloss: The old bear of the Rāmāyaṇa, who remembers everything and is the one who reminds Hanumān what he can do.

Jaḍa Bharata.gloss: A king who gave up everything he owned, and then lost it all over again for the love of one orphaned fawn.

Durgā.gloss: Assembled out of what every god had left over when none of them could win alone. She arrives already fully armed and rather calm about it.

Mahiṣāsura.gloss: The buffalo who could not be killed by any man or god — which is precisely the loophole the story walks through.

Kālī.gloss: The Devī when the fighting has gone past winning. The story is not about her rage; it is about the moment she looks down.

Annapūrṇā.gloss: Pārvatī with a ladle. The one who settles an argument about whether the world is real by turning off the kitchens.

Śākambharī.gloss: The Devī who ends a hundred-year famine by growing the food on her own body and handing it out before explaining anything.

Narakāsura.gloss: A king who asked, as he died, that the day be kept as a festival rather than as his defeat — and got it.

Bharata.gloss: Rāma's brother, handed a kingdom he never wanted by a mother who took it for him. He ruled it for fourteen years without once sitting on the chair.

Kaikeyī.gloss: Bharata's mother, who called in an old promise at the worst possible moment. The epic does not let her off, and does not make her a monster either.

Vibhīṣaṇa.gloss: Rāvaṇa's younger brother, who said so in open court, was thrown out for it, and walked across an ocean to the other side.

Ayodhyā.gloss: Rāma's city. It waits fourteen years, and on the night he is due it lights every lamp it owns because nobody is sure of the hour.

Daśaratha.gloss: Rāma's father, king of Ayodhyā. As a young man he could shoot by sound alone, and was very proud of it.

kāvaḍi.gloss: A pole carried across the shoulders with a basket hanging from each end. Pilgrims still carry them; Śravaṇa carried his parents in his.

Viṣṇu.gloss: The one who keeps things going. Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are both him, walking about in a body.

Śatākṣī.gloss: The hundred-eyed. The Devī's name for the nine nights she spent looking at a starving world before she did anything about it.

Durgama.gloss: The asura who took the Vedas away and stopped the rain for a hundred years. The Devī's name Durgā is taken from his.

Vedas.gloss: The oldest recited words — what was said over a fire, over a field, over a morning. Not books. Things known by heart, which is the only reason losing them was possible.

Kāśī.gloss: The city on the Gaṅgā that Śiva is said never to leave. Also called Varanasi, and Banaras.

māyā.gloss: The idea that what you are looking at is not quite what is there. Usually translated as illusion, which is too strong — closer to a trick of the light that goes all the way down.

Bhikṣāṭana.gloss: Śiva in his oldest job: the wanderer who goes door to door with a bowl. Not a form he chose — a penance laid on him for something he did, which is what makes queueing at his own door remarkable.

Vālmīki.gloss: The sage who wrote the Rāmāyaṇa. The first poem in the language came out of him by accident, while he was upset about a bird.

Lakṣmī.gloss: Good fortune itself, in person. She is not owned by anyone, which is the part people forget until she leaves.

Sarasvatī.gloss: Speech, learning and music. The last three nights of Navarātri are hers, which is why books and instruments are put in front of her then.

Brahmā.gloss: The one who makes things. In these stories he mostly turns up to tell someone what they have just done.

Jābālā.gloss: Satyakāma's mother, who answers a hard question about her own life plainly and tells her son to say exactly that.

Himavat.gloss: The Himālaya, as a person, and Pārvatī's father. When a mountain tells you to sit down and be sensible, it is him.

krauñca.gloss: A large water bird — usually translated curlew or heron. A pair of them are the reason the Rāmāyaṇa exists.

Hāridrumata.gloss: The teacher Satyakāma walks to. Also called Gautama — a different Gautama from the Buddha, who came much later.

Raktabīja.gloss: The asura whose name means blood-seed: every drop of his blood that reaches the ground stands up as another of him. Wounding him is the one thing that does not work.

Airāvata.gloss: Indra's white elephant, who came out of the churned ocean himself. He is the one who throws the garland down, and he is not sorry.

Vāsuki.gloss: The great snake who agreed to be used as the rope for churning the ocean. Nobody in the story asks him twice how it went.

Aparṇā.gloss: A name Pārvatī earned rather than was given: it means without even a leaf. It is what people called her after the years on the mountain.

Nandigrāma.gloss: The village outside Ayodhyā where Bharata waited fourteen years rather than live in the palace. Close enough to see the road.

Puṣpaka.gloss: The flying chariot that brings them home — taken from Rāvaṇa, who had taken it from somebody else. It goes where it is told.

Satyabhāmā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's wife, who goes to the war with him and is the one who brings Naraka down. The Bhāgavata is quite clear about whose hand it was.

cakravyūha.gloss: A battle formation shaped like a coiled wheel. Getting in is a skill; getting out again is a different skill.

Jayadratha.gloss: The king who holds the gap shut behind Abhimanyu. One man, one doorway, and the whole rest of the story turns on it.

Kuntī.gloss: Mother of the eldest three Pāṇḍavas, and of Karṇa before any of them. She kept the second fact for sixty years.

Subhadrā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's sister, Arjuna's wife, Abhimanyu's mother. In the popular telling she is the one who falls asleep halfway through the lesson.

Duḥśāsana.gloss: Duryodhana's brother. It is his son who lands the last blow on Abhimanyu.

svarga.gloss: Heaven — but a heaven you can be let into and can also walk out of again, which is what makes the last story about it interesting.

Durvāsa.gloss: A sage with a famous temper. Almost every story he is in turns on someone not paying attention to him for one second.

Nakula.gloss: The fourth Pāṇḍava, and Mādrī's son rather than Kuntī's — which is the whole reason he is the one asked for at the lake.

Sahadeva.gloss: The youngest of the five, and the first sent for water at the lake.

Mādrī.gloss: The Pāṇḍavas' other mother, and Nakula and Sahadeva's. She died long before this, which is why Yudhiṣṭhira is counting.

yakṣa.gloss: A spirit of a place — a lake, a tree, a hill. Not a god and not a demon; something that belongs to somewhere and expects to be asked.

Vidyādhara.gloss: In the Jain telling, what Rāvaṇa actually is: a human being of a line that has mastered great arts. Not a demon, and not a different kind of creature.

Vimalasūri.gloss: The Jain monk who wrote the Paumacariya, the oldest Jain Rāmāyaṇa, in Prakrit — and who opens it by saying the version everyone knows cannot be true.

Paumacariya.gloss: The Jain Rāmāyaṇa, written in Prakrit. Paüma is Padma, which is what Rāma is called in it.

Rāmāyaṇa.gloss: Rāma's journey. Vālmīki's Sanskrit poem is the oldest and the one this collection follows; there are hundreds of others, in dozens of languages.

Bhoja.gloss: An eleventh-century king of Dhārā in central India, remembered less for ruling than for the poets and scholars he kept, and for the many books that carry his name.

Gaṅgā.gloss: The river that falls from heaven. Bhagīratha brought her down; she still carries the ash of sixty thousand sons.

Sumantra.gloss: King Daśaratha's charioteer and trusted minister, who drove Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa to the forest and brought the news back to Ayodhyā.

Viśravas.gloss: Rāvaṇa's father. Jaṭāyu identifies Rāvaṇa to Rāma as the son of Viśravas.

Vaiśravaṇa.gloss: A name of Kubera, lord of wealth and Rāvaṇa's brother. Jaṭāyu uses this relationship while identifying Rāvaṇa to Rāma.

Godāvarī.gloss: The river near Pañcavaṭī in the Araṇya Kāṇḍa. Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa make water offerings for Jaṭāyu there.

Aṅgada.gloss: Son of Vālī and leader of the southern search party for Sītā. At the sea he says he can cross one hundred yojanas but is unsure he can return.

Sugrīva.gloss: King of the vānaras and Rāma's ally, who sends the search parties looking for Sītā.

Garuḍa.gloss: The mighty king of birds associated with Viṣṇu. Jāmbavān compares the strength of Hanumān's arms with Garuḍa's wings.

Meru.gloss: The great cosmic mountain. Hanumān uses circling Meru as one measure of the speed he says he can achieve.

Mahendra.gloss: The mountain Hanumān chooses as the firm launching ground for his leap across the sea toward Laṅkā.

Bharata Mahārāja.gloss: The king in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa who renounces his kingdom and later becomes attached to a fawn; distinct from Rāma's brother Bharata.

Rantideva.gloss: A king in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa remembered for giving food and finally his last drinking water to guests while he himself was hungry and thirsty.

Pṛthu.gloss: The king in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa who confronts the personified Earth over famine and then arranges for her to yield nourishment like a cow.

Naciketā.gloss: The boy in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad who waits three nights at Yama’s house and asks what happens after death.

Amarka.gloss: One of the teachers assigned to Prahlāda in his father's household.

Bhavānī.gloss: A name of Pārvatī, Śiva's consort; present beside him during the poison episode in the ocean churning.

Brahman.gloss: In the Upaniṣads, the ultimate reality on which the powers of gods and beings depend.

Earth.gloss: The Earth personified; in Pṛthu's story she takes the form of a cow and negotiates how nourishment will be drawn from her.

Hiraṇyakaśipu.gloss: Prahlāda's father, a powerful king who tries to force his son to abandon devotion to Viṣṇu.

Jātavedas.gloss: An epithet of Agni used in the Kena Upaniṣad.

Mandara.gloss: The mountain used as the churning rod when gods and asuras churn the ocean.

Mātariśvan.gloss: A name used for Vāyu in the Kena Upaniṣad.

Nārāyaṇa.gloss: A name of the Supreme Lord; in Gajendra's story he comes to the elephant king's rescue.

Nṛsiṃha.gloss: The man-lion form of Viṣṇu who appears from the pillar in Prahlāda's story.

Rukmiṇī.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's queen, present when he receives Sudāmā's humble gift.

Sunīti.gloss: Dhruva's mother, who tells him not to wish harm on those who hurt him and directs him toward the Lord.

Suruci.gloss: Dhruva's stepmother, whose words at the king's lap set his journey in motion.

Svāyambhuva Manu.gloss: The Manu used as the calf when Pṛthu draws herbs and grains from the cow-shaped Earth.

Umā Haimavatī.gloss: Umā, daughter of Himavat; in the Kena Upaniṣad she explains to Indra who the mysterious presence was.

Uttānapāda.gloss: Dhruva's father and king; his failure to intervene at the lap begins Dhruva's story.

Vājaśravas.gloss: Naciketā's father in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, whose angry words send the boy to Death.

Ṣaṇḍa.gloss: One of the teachers assigned to Prahlāda in his father's household.

Janaka.gloss: A king in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa's dūrvā episode, renowned for feeding guests and tested when Gaṇeśa arrives hungry.

dūrvā.gloss: Sacred grass used in Gaṇeśa worship. The Gaṇeśa Purāṇa devotes a sequence of chapters to its offering and merit.

Candra.gloss: The Moon as a deity. In this Gaṇeśa Purāṇa episode he laughs at Gaṇeśa, is cursed, seeks refuge and is restored.

Ambarīṣa.gloss: A king in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa who tries to honour both a fast and a guest when the two obligations collide.

Bali.gloss: The generous asura king who promises Vāmana three paces of land even after being warned what the gift may cost.

Damayantī.gloss: Princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala at her svayaṃvara even when the gods take his appearance.

Durvāsā.gloss: A formidable sage whose delayed return creates Ambarīṣa's dilemma and whose anger sets Sudarśana in pursuit.

Duryodhana.gloss: Eldest of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons and one of the Kuru princes trained by Droṇa.

Kātyāyanī.gloss: A member of Yājñavalkya's household named alongside Maitreyi when he proposes dividing his property.

Maitreyi.gloss: The questioner in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who asks whether all the wealth of the earth could make her immortal.

Niśākara.gloss: The sage in the received Sampāti sequence who foretells that Rāma's searchers will one day need Sampāti's words.

Sampāti.gloss: Jaṭāyu's elder brother, wingless when Rāma's search party finds him and able to help them through what he knows.

Satyavān.gloss: Sāvitrī's husband, whose foretold death becomes the reason she follows Yama.

Sudarśana.gloss: Viṣṇu's discus; in Ambarīṣa's story it destroys Durvāsā's attacker and then pursues the sage.

Sāvitrī.gloss: The woman in the Mahābhārata who follows Yama after Satyavān's death and keeps the conversation going through a series of boons.

Sūrya.gloss: The Sun; in Karṇa's story he warns Karṇa beforehand about Indra's intended request.

Vāmana.gloss: Viṣṇu in dwarf-brāhmaṇa form, who asks Bali for three paces of land.

Yājñavalkya.gloss: The sage in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who answers Maitreyi's question about wealth and immortality.

cūḍāmaṇi.gloss: Sītā's head-jewel, given to Hanumān as a recognition-token for Rāma.

Śukrācārya.gloss: Bali's teacher, who recognizes Vāmana as Viṣṇu and warns Bali what the promise may cost.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra.gloss: The blind king of Hastināpura and father of Duryodhana and his brothers.

Drupada.gloss: King of Pañcāla, remembered in Droṇa's story as the ruler against whom Droṇa later sends his pupils.

Citrakūṭa.gloss: The forested place where Rāma and Sītā lived during part of the exile; Sītā recalls a private episode from there for Hanumān to carry back.

Sutala.gloss: The realm given to Bali after the three-step episode, where Viṣṇu promises him protection.

Yamunā.gloss: The river where Durvāsā goes to bathe after accepting Ambarīṣa's invitation to eat.

Mahābhārata.gloss: The Sanskrit epic of the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas. These stories cite a specific parva and passage rather than treating every later retelling as the same witness.

Vidarbha.gloss: Damayantī's kingdom in the Nalopākhyāna of the Mahābhārata.

Niṣadha.gloss: The kingdom ruled by Nala in the Nalopākhyāna of the Mahābhārata.

Aśoka.gloss: The aśoka tree. Sītā is found in an aśoka grove in Laṅkā in the Sundara Kāṇḍa.

Bhāgavata.gloss: Short form of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the Sanskrit Purāṇa used for several stories in this collection.

Vyāsa.gloss: The sage traditionally associated with arranging the Vedas and composing the Mahābhārata.

Bhārata.gloss: A traditional short name for the Mahābhārata in its transmitted opening.

Śuka.gloss: Vyāsa's son, named in the transmitted Mahābhārata opening among those who know the difficult verses.

Sañjaya.gloss: The narrator who reports the Kurukṣetra war to Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the Mahābhārata.

Kubera.gloss: The lord of wealth in Sanskrit tradition, also called Vaiśravaṇa.

Bhṛgu.gloss: An ancient sage. In Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.89 he is sent to test Brahmā, Śiva and Viṣṇu.

Vaikuṇṭha.gloss: The divine abode of Viṣṇu in Vaiṣṇava tradition.

darbha.gloss: A sacred grass used in Vedic and ritual contexts.

Puṉitavati.gloss: The name Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār was born with, and the one nobody uses any more.

Kōtai.gloss: Āṇḍāḷ's name before she was Āṇḍāḷ. She signs it herself at the end of the Tiruppāvai.

Śrīvilliputtūr.gloss: Āṇḍāḷ's town in the far south of Tamil Nadu, where the garland is still worn by her first.

Poygai.gloss: First of the twelve Āḻvārs, and the first into the doorway. Poygai means a pond.

Bhūtam.gloss: Second of the Āḻvārs, who pointed out that where one can lie down, two can sit.

Pēy.gloss: Third of the Āḻvārs. The name means somebody taken over by something — how he was about God, and he kept it.

Tirukkōvalūr.gloss: The town with the doorway. Its lord is Trivikrama, and his other name there means lord of the threshold.

Madhurakavi.gloss: The Āḻvār who wrote eleven verses, all of them about his teacher and none about God.

Tirukkurukūr.gloss: Nammāḻvār's town on the Tāmiraparaṇi, called Āḻvārtirunagari now. The tamarind is still there.

Nandanār.gloss: The Nāyaṉār who made the drums the temples played on. Also called Tirunāḷaippōvār, the one who will go tomorrow.

Tiruppuṅkūr.gloss: The temple where the stone bull sits off to one side instead of in the middle of the way.

Tiruppāṇāḻvār.gloss: The singer of Śrīraṅgam, who sang from the far bank and was carried in. His ten verses are the Amalanādipirāṉ.

Raṅganātha.gloss: Viṣṇu asleep on his serpent at Śrīraṅgam, lying down rather than standing, and very old.

Kāvēri.gloss: The great river of the Tamil country. Śrīraṅgam sits on an island in it.

Kaṭha Upaniṣad.gloss: The Upaniṣad in which a boy named Naciketā goes to the house of death and will not leave without an answer. It is where the chariot picture comes from.

Ṛgveda.gloss: The oldest of the four Vedas — a collection of hymns, some of them riddles. Several famous Upaniṣadic lines are already sitting in it.

Dīrghatamas.gloss: The seer of a long hymn of riddles in the Ṛgveda, the hymn that holds the verse about the two birds.

pippala.gloss: The fruit of the fig — the word the verse uses for what the eating bird is eating. The tree itself is never named.

Mārkaṇḍeya.gloss: A sage who lives long enough to be the only one left when the world dissolves, and who asked to be shown that on purpose.

Nara.gloss: One of a pair of sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who appear together and are understood as two forms of one presence.

Vidura.gloss: Half-brother to the blind king and the one person in that court who says the true thing every time, and is listened to by nobody who matters.

Sātyaki.gloss: A warrior of Kṛṣṇa's own people who goes with him as his second, and who finds out about the plan to seize him.

Gāndhārī.gloss: Queen of Hastināpura and Duryodhana's mother, who tied a cloth over her own eyes when she married a blind husband.

Hastināpura.gloss: The Kuru capital, where the blind king holds his court and where the war is decided on before it is fought.

Bhīṣma.gloss: The grand-uncle of both sides, bound by an old vow to whoever holds the throne — which is why he is always in the room and never able to stop anything.

Rādhā.gloss: Karṇa's mother — the woman who lifted him out of the river and raised him. Not the Rādhā of the Vraja stories; a different woman with the same name.

Adhiratha.gloss: A charioteer by trade, and Karṇa's father — the man who found the box on the water and took the child home the same hour.

Manu.gloss: The first man of an age — and, because each one presides over an age, also the name of that stretch of time. Fourteen of them make one day of Brahmā.

Rudra.gloss: An ancient name of Śiva — the one who howls, the one in the storm.

Yaśodā.gloss: The mother who raises Kṛṣṇa in the cowherd household.

Fierce-Howl.gloss: The jackal in Ryder’s telling of The Blue Jackal. Fierce-Howl is the translator’s English name.

Naduk.gloss: The travelling merchant in Arthur Ryder’s telling of The Mice That Ate Iron. This name follows that translation.

Hari.gloss: A name of Viṣṇu, also used for Kṛṣṇa.

Syamantaka.gloss: The radiant jewel at the centre of this story, associated with Sūrya and with extraordinary prosperity when kept properly.

Satrājit.gloss: A Yādava devotee of Sūrya who receives the Syamantaka jewel and chooses to keep it.

Prasena.gloss: Satrājit's brother, killed by a lion while hunting with the Syamantaka jewel.

Dvārakā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's city, where the accusation about Prasena and the Syamantaka jewel spreads.

Ugrasena.gloss: King of the Yādavas. Kṛṣṇa says a jewel of such public value should properly be placed with him.

Jāmbavatī.gloss: Jāmbavān's daughter, whom Kṛṣṇa marries after the Syamantaka jewel is recovered.

Amar-Nīti.gloss: A merchant-devotee in the Periya Purāṇam, remembered for the balance on which a single loincloth outweighed his wealth.

Sundarar.gloss: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint whose first hymn begins at Tiruvennainallur after the old-man-and-deed episode.

Appar.gloss: Tirunāvukkaracar, the Tamil Śaiva poet-saint repeatedly remembered with an uzhavaram in his hand.

Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār.gloss: One of the Āḻvārs; his own Periya Tirumoḻi remembers a transformed past, while later hagiography tells the highway-robbery conversion scene.

Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār.gloss: King-poet of the Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi, remembered in later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography as trying to send his army into the Rāmāyaṇa.

Bhairava.gloss: A fierce form of Śiva summoned in the Liṅgodbhava telling to confront Brahmā after the false claim.

Ketakī.gloss: The fragrant ketakī flower that becomes a witness in the Liṅgodbhava story.

Aṃśumān.gloss: King Sagara’s grandson, who learns what is needed to free his uncles after their destruction.

Bhagīratha.gloss: The king whose long effort brings Gaṅgā from heaven to the earth and to his ancestors.

Bhāgīrathī.gloss: A name for Gaṅgā that remembers Bhagīratha’s work to bring her down.

Dilīpa.gloss: Bhagīratha’s father, who sought to complete the work begun for their ancestors.

Gokarṇa.gloss: The place where Bhagīratha practises tapas in the Gaṅgā-descent account.

Jahnu.gloss: The sage who drinks the flooding Gaṅgā and later releases her, giving her the name Jāhnavī.

Jāhnavī.gloss: A name for Gaṅgā after she flows out again from the sage Jahnu.

Sagara.gloss: The king whose sons’ fate begins the generations-long quest to bring Gaṅgā down.

Aśvins.gloss: The twin divine physicians who offer to restore the sage Cyavana’s youth.

Cyavana.gloss: The sage living in an anthill whom Sukanyā accidentally hurts and later marries.

Sukanyā.gloss: King Śaryāti’s daughter, whose encounter with Cyavana and the Aśvin twins tests her discernment.

Śaryāti.gloss: The king and father of Sukanyā in the Cyavana episode.

Svabhāvakṛpaṇa.gloss: The brahmin in the Pañcatantra who imagines a fortune from one jar of barley-meal.

Nandī.gloss: Śiva’s attendant who bars Rāvaṇa from crossing Kailāsa and warns him about the pride of his strength.

Nṛga.gloss: A king who became a lizard after a disputed gift.

Virocana.gloss: An asura seeker in the Chāndogya dialogue.

Prajāpati.gloss: The teacher approached by Indra and Virocana.

Kauśika.gloss: The brahmin who meets the Dharma-vyādha.

Maināka.gloss: The mountain that offers Hanumān rest.

Śumbha.gloss: The asura king who sends a messenger to the Devī.

Kauśikī.gloss: The radiant Goddess emerging from Pārvatī.

Kālikā.gloss: The dark form named in Devī Māhātmya chapter 5.

Caṇḍa.gloss: One of the asuras who reports the Goddess to Śumbha.

Muṇḍa.gloss: One of the asuras who reports the Goddess to Śumbha.

Dhūmralocana.gloss: The commander sent to seize the Goddess.

Sugrīva (Devī messenger).gloss: Śumbha’s messenger in the Devī Māhātmya, distinct from Rāma’s ally.

Mithilā.gloss: The city where Kauśika meets the Dharma-vyādha.

Uccaiḥśravas.gloss: The celestial horse named among Śumbha’s claimed treasures.

Devī.gloss: The Goddess, speaking in this episode of the Devī Māhātmya.

Ṛbhu.gloss: Nidāgha's teacher, a son of Brahmā in this Viṣṇu Purāṇa account.

Nidāgha.gloss: Ṛbhu's pupil; a son of Pulastya in this account.

Devīkā.gloss: The river beside Nidāgha's grove in Viṣṇu Purāṇa II.15–16.

Pulastya.gloss: A sage named as Nidāgha's father in this account.

Vāsudeva.gloss: A name of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa. Here Ṛbhu names the undivided nature of the universe Vāsudeva. Distinct from Vasudeva, Kṛṣṇa's father.

Upakosala.gloss: Upakosala Kāmalāyana, the pupil taught by the fires and then Satyakāma in Chāndogya 4.10–15.

Gārhapatya.gloss: The household sacred fire; the first fire to give its individual teaching in this episode.

Anvāhāryapacana.gloss: The second sacred fire to give its teaching in Chāndogya 4.12, also associated with the southern fire.

Āhavanīya.gloss: The offering fire; third in the sequence of individual teachings in Chāndogya 4.13.

Mudgala.gloss: A gleaning ascetic who asks about heaven's disadvantages and chooses liberation in this Mahābhārata episode.

Kurukṣetra.gloss: The region where Mudgala gathers grain in this episode.

Jājali.gloss: The ascetic who shelters nesting birds and later visits Tulādhāra in the Mahābhārata.

Tulādhāra.gloss: The trader whose teaching begins with friendliness, even regard and the least necessary harm.

Gārgī.gloss: Gārgī Vācaknavī, the woman scholar who asks about ākāśa and Akṣara in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.

Videha.gloss: A kingdom named with Kāśī in Gārgī's warrior comparison.

Akṣara.gloss: The imperishable in Yājñavalkya's teaching. In other contexts akṣara also means a syllable; that is not the meaning here.

Ākāśa.gloss: Space, or ether in older translations. This gloss is not an identification with a modern scientific substance.
